newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: International labour leaders leave South Korea.
newsitem.headline: International labour leaders leave South Korea.

text.p: Four international labour leaders visiting Seoul to show support for strikers said they were leaving on Thursday after an official warning by immigration police not to meet union leaders.
A last-minute tour of Daewoo Group factories was cancelled, according to Marcello Malentacchi, head of the International Metalworkers' Federation.
"I think Daewoo management must have been warned that our visit could cause unfriendly action by the government," he said just before leaving for the airport.
"We first issued them a polite verbal warning that their activities violated our immigration law," Yoo Byong-kwang, a director general at the Justice Ministry, told Reuters.
"But they took part in protests in Myongdong and a mass rally despite the warning so we had to deliver a formal letter saying they would be deported unless they stopped these activities," he said.

Malentacchi said he had planned to leave on Friday, although the other three were originally scheduled to fly out on Thursday. "I wanted to visit Hyundai factories in Ulsan today, but I was afraid to cause trouble," he said.
The southeast city of Ulsan has been a focal point of opposition to a controversial three-week old labour law that has triggered wildcat stoppages nationwide.
Immigration police gave the mission a verbal warning against support for union leaders on Monday.
The mission received on Wednesday a second call at their hotel by a senior immigration official, who relayed a letter outlining the laws he and the other three would violate if they met union bosses.
Malentacchi said the immigration official told them: "Any participation or contact with Korean union leaders would be considered in violation of the law and result in deportation."

He warned South Korea's reputation would suffer if there was a crackdown on union leaders who are demanding the government repeal the law, which allows companies to dismiss workers and replace strikers.
"The stance the government has taken since this law was passed has even hardened. This will be embarrassing for South Korea's reputation," he said.
The mission has irked the government with regular visits to Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral where strike leaders are sheltering from arrest and by appearing as star guests at several worker rallies.
